exam: A 58‑year‑old man with hypertension presents with sudden back pain and a blood pressure difference of 30 mmHg between arms – what is your immediate management step? — Recognise possible type B dissection, start IV beta‑blocker, obtain urgent CT angiography, arrange transfer if complications arise.

Explain how you would differentiate a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm from a perforated duodenal ulcer in a low‑resource setting. — Look for pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension, and rapid expansion; use bedside ultrasound to identify aortic diameter ≥5 cm versus free intraperitoneal fluid without aortic wall defect.

Why is a statin recommended for a patient with an aortic aneurysm even if cholesterol is normal? — Statins stabilize atherosclerotic plaque, reduce inflammation, and slow aneurysm growth independent of lipid levels.

A patient with known Marfan syndrome has a 4.8 cm thoracic aortic diameter on CT. What factors influence the decision for elective surgery? — Size threshold, rate of growth >0.5 cm/6 months, family history of dissection, and symptomatic status guide timing.

What are the contraindications to using thrombolysis in a patient with suspected aortic dissection? — Thrombolysis can worsen bleeding into the false lumen and precipitate rupture; it is avoided in any suspected dissection.

Describe the role of antibiotics in managing a mycotic aortic aneurysm and the steps if cultures are negative. — Start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin) pending cultures; if cultures remain negative, continue empiric therapy based on likely organisms and arrange surgical debridement.

How does coarctation of the aorta present differently in an adult versus a child, and what is the first-line treatment in a low‑resource hospital? — Adults often have hypertension and weak femoral pulses; children may have heart failure. Initial treatment is blood pressure control with beta‑blockers, followed by referral for surgical or balloon angioplasty.

A patient with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm reports new hoarseness. What complication should you suspect and why? — Hoarseness may indicate a thoracic aneurysm compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner’s syndrome) or impending rupture; urgent imaging is required.
ai.title: Aortic Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Aortic disease includes aneurysm, dissection and coarctation. It is diagnosed by imaging, staged by size or extent, and managed with surgery or medical therapy. In low‑resource settings, clinical clues guide urgent decisions.

b: Aneurysm: focal dilatation ≥ 1.5 × normal diameter
Dissection: intimal tear creating true and false lumen
Coarctation: congenital narrowing, usually juxtaductal
sections.p: Aortic disease refers to any structural abnormality of the aorta that threatens its integrity or flow. Diagnosis relies on imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) and clinical signs when imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Detect size of aneurysm or presence of dissection when CT unavailable; a diameter ≥ 5 cm suggests surgical referral
Gold standard for extent of dissection and aneurysm morphology; shows true vs false lumen
Alternative to CT for radiation‑sensitive patients; provides same anatomic detail
Screening tool; widened mediastinum > 8 cm suggests possible dissection

b: Aneurysm: <5 cm (monitor), 5–5.5 cm (consider surgery), >5.5 cm (surgical repair)
Dissection type A (ascending) = surgical emergency; type B (descending) = medical unless complications
Coarctation: gradient ≥ 20 mmHg or systemic hypertension
sections.p: Aneurysms are staged by maximal diameter; dissections by Stanford (type A vs B) or DeBakey classification; coarctation by pressure gradient.

b: Atherosclerotic degeneration – most common in adults >60 y

Connective‑tissue disorders – Marfan, Ehlers‑Danlos (younger patients)

sections.p: In East Africa, atherosclerosis, hypertension, and infectious aortitis dominate. Consider tropical infections and systemic diseases.

b: Aneurysm: pulsatile abdominal mass, back pain, hoarseness (thoracic)
Dissection: abrupt tearing chest or back pain, unequal blood pressures, new murmur of aortic regurgitation
Coarctation: upper‑body hypertension, diminished femoral pulses, rib notching on X‑ray
sections.p: Presentation varies with type. Aneurysms are often silent until rupture; dissection causes sudden tearing chest/back pain; coarctation presents with hypertension and weak lower‑extremity pulses.

b: Blood pressure in both arms – >20 mmHg difference suggests dissection or coarctation
Peripheral pulses – absent or delayed femoral pulse points to coarctation or dissection
sections.p: Prioritise bedside tools when imaging is limited. Use clinical scoring to decide urgency.

Elevated in infectious aortitis; normal values do not exclude chronic atherosclerotic disease
Positive cultures guide antibiotic choice in mycotic aneurysm

Rapid aneurysm growth >0.5 cm in 6 months

b: Beta‑blockers (e.g., labetalol) – lower shear stress, first‑line for dissection and aneurysm control
Statins – stabilize atherosclerotic plaque, reduce aneurysm expansion
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for mycotic aneurysm until culture‑directed therapy
Urgent surgical repair for type A dissection, ruptured aneurysm, or aneurysm >5.5 cm
Endovascular stent grafting – preferred when open surgery not feasible
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control blood pressure, and arrange definitive repair when possible.

Smoking cessation, lipid control, and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus
sections.p: Regular imaging and risk‑factor control are essential.
